units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Solving quadratic equations
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Mathematics, Term 1: Equations and inequalities (solve quadratic equations by factorisation and the quadratic formula; nature of roots)
units.intention: Today I am solving quadratic equations by factorising and with the formula.
units.prompt: How do you choose between factorising and the formula?

lesson.say: A quadratic equation can be written as a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero. Always get it into this form first.
lesson.html:
ax² + bx + c = 0

Move every term to one side so the other side is zero.

lesson.say: If x squared minus five x plus six equals zero, factorise to x minus two times x minus three equals zero. So x equals two or x equals three.
lesson.html:
x² − 5x + 6 = 0→(x − 2)(x − 3) = 0→x = 2 or x = 3

If a product is zero, one of the factors must be zero.

lesson.say: When it will not factorise easily, use the formula: x equals negative b, plus or minus the square root of b squared minus four a c, all over two a.
lesson.html:
x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a

b² − 4ac is the discriminant. If it is negative, there are no real roots.

example.q: Solve x² + 2x − 15 = 0.
steps: Find two numbers that multiply to −15 and add to 2: 5 and −3.

questions.q: Solve: x² − 9x + 20 = 0
questions.explain: x = 4 or x = 5.

questions.q: Solve: x² = 49
What is the discriminant of x² + 4x + 5 = 0?
What does a negative discriminant tell you?
hints: You'd take the square root of a negative.
questions.explain: A negative discriminant means no real roots.

questions.q: Solve: 2x² − 8x = 0
questions.explain: x = 0 or x = 4.

units.parent: Your child solved quadratic equations by factorising and using the quadratic formula.
units.teacher: Shows solving quadratics by factorisation and formula, and interpreting the discriminant.
units.done: Set the equation to zero, then factorise or use the formula.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Growth and decay
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Mathematics, Term 4: Finance, growth and decay (simple and compound decay; straight-line and reducing-balance depreciation; nominal and effective rates)
units.intention: Today I am calculating how value grows and falls over time.
units.prompt: Why do cars lose value faster in the first years?

lesson.say: With compound growth, A equals P times one plus i, to the power n. P is the starting amount, i is the rate as a decimal, and n is the number of periods.
lesson.html:
A = P(1 + i)ⁿ

Savings and populations can grow this way.

lesson.say: In straight-line depreciation, the value drops by the same amount each year. A equals P times one minus i n.
lesson.html:
A = P(1 − in)

A R100 000 machine losing 10% a year: R10 000 every year.

lesson.say: In reducing-balance depreciation, the value drops by a percentage of what is left. A equals P times one minus i, to the power n. Cars often lose value this way.
lesson.html:
A = P(1 − i)ⁿ

The amount lost gets smaller each year.

example.q: A R200 000 car depreciates at 15% per year, reducing balance. What is it worth after 2 years?

questions.q: Which formula is reducing-balance depreciation?
questions.explain: A = P(1 − i)ⁿ.

questions.q: R10 000 machine, straight-line depreciation at 10% per year. Value after 3 years?
R5 000 grows at 10% compound per year. Value after 2 years?
Why does reducing-balance lose less each year?
options: The percentage is taken from a smaller value
hints: But what is it a percentage of?
questions.explain: The same percentage of a smaller value is a smaller amount.

questions.q: Which is an example of decay?
questions.explain: A phone losing value is decay.

units.parent: Your child calculated compound growth and straight-line and reducing-balance depreciation.
units.teacher: Shows selecting and applying growth and decay formulas in financial contexts.
units.done: Growth adds a percentage; depreciation removes one, straight-line or reducing-balance.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Circle geometry
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Mathematics, Term 3: Euclidean geometry (circle theorems: perpendicular from centre bisects chord; angle at centre; angles in the same segment; cyclic quadrilaterals; tangents)
units.intention: Today I am using circle theorems to find unknown angles.
units.prompt: Which theorem do you find easiest to spot in a diagram?

lesson.say: The angle at the centre of a circle is double the angle at the circumference, when both stand on the same arc.
lesson.html:
∠ centre = 2 × ∠ circumference

If the angle at the circumference is 40°, the angle at the centre is 80°.

lesson.h: Angles in a semicircle and same segment
lesson.say: The angle in a semicircle is ninety degrees. Angles in the same segment, standing on the same chord, are equal.
lesson.html: ∠ in semicircle = 90°→∠s in same segment are equal

lesson.say: In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles add up to one hundred and eighty degrees. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
lesson.html:
Opposite ∠s of cyclic quad = 180°→Tangent ⊥ radius

Always give the reason for each step.

example.q: In a cyclic quadrilateral, one angle is 75°. What is the opposite angle?
steps: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.

questions.q: The angle at the circumference is 35°. What is the angle at the centre on the same arc?
What is the angle in a semicircle?
questions.explain: The angle in a semicircle is 90°.

questions.q: In a cyclic quadrilateral, one angle is 112°. Find the opposite angle.
What angle does a tangent make with the radius at the point of contact?
questions.explain: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius.

questions.q: Two angles stand on the same chord in the same segment. One is 50°. The other is …
questions.explain: Angles in the same segment are equal.

units.parent: Your child used circle theorems to find unknown angles.
units.teacher: Shows applying circle theorems with reasons: angle at centre, semicircle, same segment, cyclic quadrilateral, tangent-radius.
units.done: Spot the theorem in the diagram, apply it, and give the reason.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Interest, loans and inflation
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Mathematical Literacy: Finance (simple and compound interest; loans and investments; the effect of inflation)
units.intention: Today I am working out interest and the real cost of borrowing.
units.prompt: Why might a shop offer to let you pay later?

lesson.say: Simple interest is worked out on the starting amount only. R1 000 at 10 percent a year earns R100 every year.
lesson.html:
R1 000→R1 100→R1 200→R1 300

Simple interest: the same R100 every year.

lesson.say: With compound interest, each year's interest is added on, so next year you also earn interest on the interest.
lesson.html:
R1 000→R1 100→R1 210→R1 331

10% compound for 3 years: R1 331.

lesson.say: When you borrow, interest works against you. Store cards and short-term loans often charge high interest, so you can pay back much more than you borrowed. Inflation means prices rise over time, so money buys less.
lesson.html: Compare the total cost of a loan, not only the monthly payment.

example.q: You invest R5 000 at 8% simple interest per year. How much do you have after 3 years?

questions.q: R2 000 earns 5% simple interest per year. How much interest is earned after 4 years, in rand?
questions.explain: R100 a year × 4 years = R400.

questions.q: R1 000 earns 10% compound interest per year. How much is there after 2 years, in rand?
Why does compound interest grow faster than simple interest?
options: You earn interest on earlier interest too
hints: What is the interest worked out on?
questions.explain: Each year's interest is added, so it earns interest too.

questions.q: Inflation is 5% a year. A loaf of bread costs R20 now. About how much will it cost in a year?
questions.explain: 5% of R20 = R1, so about R21.

questions.q: Two loans of R10 000. Loan A: R950 a month for 12 months. Loan B: R620 a month for 24 months. Which costs less in total?
questions.explain: Loan A costs R11 400 in total; Loan B costs R14 880. The smaller monthly payment costs more overall.

options: Seeing the amounts year by year

units.parent: Your child compared simple and compound interest, and the real cost of loans.
units.teacher: Shows calculating simple and compound interest, interpreting inflation, and comparing the total cost of credit.
units.done: Compound interest grows on itself. Always compare the total cost of a loan.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Fencing, tiling and tanks
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Mathematical Literacy: Measurement (perimeter, area and volume of rectangles, circles, rectangular prisms and cylinders; using given formulas in real contexts)
units.intention: Today I am using perimeter, area and volume for real jobs.
units.prompt: Which job at home needs measuring first?

lesson.say: Perimeter is the distance around a shape, like fencing a garden. Area is the space inside, like tiles for a floor. Area is measured in square units.
lesson.html:
Perimeter: around (m)→Area: inside (m²)

Rectangle: perimeter = 2 × (l + b), area = l × b

lesson.say: For a circle, the circumference is pi times the diameter, and the area is pi times the radius squared. Use 3.14 for pi.
lesson.html: C = π × d→A = π × r²→π ≈ 3,14

lesson.say: Volume is the space a container holds. For a box, multiply length by breadth by height. For a cylinder, multiply the area of the circle by the height. One cubic metre holds 1 000 litres.
lesson.html: Box: l × b × h→Cylinder: π × r² × h→1 m³ = 1 000 ℓ

example.q: A water tank is a cylinder with radius 1 m and height 2 m. How many litres does it hold? Use π = 3,14.

questions.q: A room is 4 m by 3 m. What is its floor area, in m²?
How many metres of fencing go around a garden 8 m by 5 m?
Find the area of a circle with radius 10 cm, in cm². Use π = 3,14.
A box is 50 cm long, 20 cm wide and 10 cm high. What is its volume, in cm³?
You want to tile a floor. What do you need to work out?
questions.explain: Tiles cover the area of the floor.

options: Knowing which measurement the job needs

units.parent: Your child worked out perimeter, area and volume for real jobs like fencing, tiling and water tanks.
units.teacher: Shows selecting and using given formulas for perimeter, area and volume, and converting between cubic metres and litres.
units.done: Around: perimeter. Inside: area. What it holds: volume.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Floor plans and travel time
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Mathematical Literacy: Maps, plans and other representations (floor plans and symbols; scale calculations; planning routes; distance, speed and time)
units.intention: Today I am reading floor plans and working out travel times.
units.prompt: How do you decide when to leave for a trip?

lesson.say: A floor plan shows a building from above. It uses symbols for doors, windows and walls, and has a scale so you can work out real sizes.
lesson.html: A door is often drawn as a line with a quarter circle, showing which way it opens.

lesson.say: On a plan with a scale of 1 to 100, 1 centimetre on paper is 1 metre in real life. Measure on the plan, then multiply.
lesson.html: 1 : 100→1 cm on paper→= 1 m real

lesson.say: Distance equals speed times time. A taxi travelling at 60 kilometres per hour for 2 hours covers 120 kilometres. Time equals distance divided by speed.
lesson.html:
D = S × T→T = D ÷ S→S = D ÷ T

0,5 hours = 30 minutes; 0,25 hours = 15 minutes.

example.q: A route on a map is 90 km. A bus averages 60 km/h. How long does the trip take?

questions.q: Scale 1 : 100. A bedroom is 3,5 cm long on the plan. How long is it really, in metres?
A car travels at 80 km/h for 3 hours. How far does it go, in km?
A trip is 150 km at 100 km/h. How long does it take?
questions.explain: 1,5 hours = 1 hour 30 minutes, not 1 hour 50 minutes.

questions.q: What does a floor plan show?
questions.explain: A floor plan is a view from above, showing the rooms.

questions.q: A learner says 0,25 hours is 25 minutes. Is that right?

units.parent: Your child read floor plans and worked out real sizes and travel times.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting floor plans and symbols, applying scale, and using distance, speed and time, including converting decimal hours.
units.done: Use the scale for real sizes, and D = S × T for trips. An hour has 60 minutes.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Graphs that tell the truth
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Mathematical Literacy: Data handling (bar graphs, pie charts and line graphs; choosing a suitable graph; recognising misleading graphs)
units.intention: Today I am choosing the right graph and spotting misleading ones.
units.prompt: Have you seen a graph in an advert? Did you trust it?

lesson.say: Use a bar graph to compare groups, a pie chart to show parts of a whole, and a line graph to show change over time.
lesson.html: Compare groups: bar→Parts of a whole: pie→Change over time: line

lesson.say: A whole pie is 360 degrees, or 100 percent. If 25 percent of a budget goes on food, its slice is a quarter of the circle, 90 degrees.
lesson.html: 100% = 360°→25% = 90°→1% = 3,6°

lesson.say: A graph can mislead if the vertical axis does not start at zero, if the scale jumps, or if pictures are stretched. Always read the numbers, not only the shape.
lesson.html: A small rise looks huge when the axis starts at 95 instead of 0.

example.q: A household spends R3 000 of its R12 000 income on rent. How many degrees is the rent slice in a pie chart?
steps: The rent slice is 90°, a quarter of the circle.

questions.q: Which graph best shows how the price of petrol changed over 12 months?
hints: The question is about change over time.
questions.explain: Line graphs show change over time.

questions.q: Which graph best shows how a budget is split between food, rent and transport?
hints: The parts make up one whole budget.
questions.explain: A pie chart shows parts of a whole.

questions.q: In a pie chart, a slice is 50% of the whole. How many degrees is it?
A bar graph of sales starts its vertical axis at 950 instead of 0. What is the danger?
hints: The bottoms of the bars are cut off.
What happens to differences between bars?
questions.explain: Cutting off the axis makes small differences look large.

questions.q: A slice of a pie chart is 72°. What percentage of the whole is that? (Type the number only.)

options: Matching the graph to the question

units.parent: Your child chose suitable graphs and spotted ways that graphs can mislead.
units.teacher: Shows selecting appropriate representations, calculating pie chart angles, and critically evaluating misleading graphs.
units.done: Choose the graph that fits the question, and always check the axis.

units.subject: Mathematical Literacy
units.title: Comparing risks
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Mathematical Literacy: Probability (two-way tables; tree diagrams for two events; interpreting risk in health, games and insurance)
units.intention: Today I am comparing risks fairly, using tables and tree diagrams.
units.prompt: How do people decide whether something is risky?

lesson.say: A two-way table sorts data by two things at once, for example whether people were vaccinated, and whether they got flu. Of 200 vaccinated people, 10 got flu. Of 200 unvaccinated people, 40 got flu.
lesson.html:
Vaccinated: 10 of 200 got flu.

Not vaccinated: 40 of 200 got flu.

lesson.say: To compare groups fairly, compare probabilities, not only counts. 10 out of 200 is 5 percent. 40 out of 200 is 20 percent. The unvaccinated group had four times the risk.
lesson.html:
10 ÷ 200 = 5%→40 ÷ 200 = 20%

Percentages let you compare groups of different sizes too.

lesson.say: A tree diagram lists every outcome of two events. Tossing two coins gives four outcomes: heads heads, heads tails, tails heads and tails tails. The chance of two heads is 1 out of 4.
lesson.html:
HH→HT→TH→TT

P(two heads) = 1/4

example.q: Of all 400 people above, 10 + 40 got flu. What is the probability that a person picked at random got flu?

questions.q: 200 vaccinated people: 10 got flu. What percentage got flu? (Type the number only.)
200 unvaccinated people: 40 got flu. What percentage got flu? (Type the number only.)
From these results, which group had the higher risk of flu?
questions.explain: 20% is higher than 5%.

questions.q: Two coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting one head and one tail?
hints: List the outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT.
questions.explain: HT and TH: 2 out of 4 = 1/2.

questions.q: Why compare percentages instead of counts?
options: The groups may be different sizes
hints: Imagine 10 sick out of 50, and 20 sick out of 1 000.
questions.explain: Percentages make groups of different sizes comparable.

options: Reading the table row by row

units.parent: Your child used two-way tables and tree diagrams to compare risks fairly.
units.teacher: Shows reading two-way tables, comparing relative risk using percentages, and listing outcomes with tree diagrams.
units.done: Compare risks with percentages, and list every outcome before you count.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Drama: The Inheritance
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 English Home Language: Literature (drama: stage directions, dialogue, aside, dramatic irony, tension, characterisation; contextual questions)
units.intention: Today I am analysing how a playwright builds tension and character.
units.prompt: Should Mandla read the last line? Why?
units.passage:
The Inheritance (a 2to.iQ drama extract)

(A small kitchen in Gqeberha. MANDLA, 17, sits at the table with an envelope. His older sister, ZODWA, enters with shopping bags.)

ZODWA: You opened it.

MANDLA: (not looking up) It's addressed to both of us.

ZODWA: And? What did Tata leave us? His debts?

MANDLA: The house. And a letter. He says he's sorry.

(Silence. ZODWA puts the bags down slowly.)

ZODWA: Sorry. Twelve years, and he's sorry. (She laughs, but it cracks.) Read it to me.

MANDLA: (aside) If I read her the last line, she'll never forgive him. If I don't, she'll never forgive me.

lesson.say: Read the extract, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
The Inheritance (a 2to.iQ drama extract)

(A small kitchen in Gqeberha. MANDLA, 17, sits at the table with an envelope. His older sister, ZODWA, enters with shopping bags.)

ZODWA: You opened it.

MANDLA: (not looking up) It's addressed to both of us.

ZODWA: And? What did Tata leave us? His debts?

MANDLA: The house. And a letter. He says he's sorry.

(Silence. ZODWA puts the bags down slowly.)

ZODWA: Sorry. Twelve years, and he's sorry. (She laughs, but it cracks.) Read it to me.

MANDLA: (aside) If I read her the last line, she'll never forgive him. If I don't, she'll never forgive me.

lesson.say: Stage directions, in italics and brackets, tell actors how to move and speak. Not looking up shows Mandla avoiding his sister. She laughs, but it cracks shows hidden pain.
lesson.html:
(not looking up) → avoidance

(She laughs, but it cracks.) → hidden pain

lesson.say: An aside is spoken to the audience, and other characters cannot hear it. Mandla's aside creates dramatic irony: we know there is a painful last line, but Zodwa does not.
lesson.html:
Aside: to the audience→Dramatic irony: we know more than a character

This creates tension.

example.q: What does Zodwa's question His debts? reveal about her?
steps: She expects the worst from her father.
Her tone is bitter and sarcastic.
She has been hurt by him and does not trust him.

questions.q: What is an aside?
options: Words spoken to the audience that other characters do not hear
A long speech to another character
hints: Mandla says something only we hear.
questions.explain: An aside is heard by the audience, not by other characters.

questions.q: What creates dramatic irony in this extract?
options: We know about the last line, but Zodwa does not
questions.explain: The audience knows something Zodwa does not.

questions.q: What does Twelve years, and he's sorry suggest?
options: The father has been absent for a long time
questions.explain: It suggests the father was absent for twelve years.

questions.q: What is the mood at the end of the extract?
questions.explain: The unresolved dilemma creates tension.

questions.q: Why does ZODWA put the bags down slowly?
questions.explain: The slow movement shows shock at the news.

reflect.q: How did you analyse the extract?

units.parent: Your child analysed a drama extract for stage directions, an aside and dramatic irony.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting stage directions, characterisation, aside and dramatic irony, and their effect on tension.
units.done: Stage directions, asides and dramatic irony build character and tension.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: CV and covering letter
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 English Home Language: Writing and Presenting (transactional texts: CV, covering letter, formal letter; register and format)
units.intention: Today I am learning to write a clear CV and covering letter.
units.prompt: What would you put in your own CV right now?

lesson.say: A CV is a short summary of you: contact details, a short profile, education, skills, experience, achievements and references. Keep it to one or two pages.
lesson.html:
Contact→Profile→Education→Skills→Experience→References

Volunteering and school leadership count as experience.

lesson.say: A covering letter introduces you for a specific job. Say which job you are applying for, why you are suitable, and ask for an interview. Use a formal register.
lesson.html:
Address and date→Greeting→Why this job→Why me→Closing

Tailor it to each job.

lesson.say: Use formal language, no slang, and a professional email address. Check spelling twice and ask someone to read it.
lesson.html:
Formal→Clear→Checked

A single spelling mistake can lose you an interview.

example.q: Which email address is best for a CV: coolkid2000@mail.com or n.dlamini@mail.com?
steps: A CV needs to look professional.

questions.q: How long should a school-leaver's CV usually be?
questions.explain: One or two pages is best.

questions.q: Which belongs in a covering letter?
options: Why you are suitable for this job
questions.explain: Explain why you suit the specific job.

questions.q: Which sentence suits a covering letter?
options: I am writing to apply for the position of junior administrator.
questions.explain: It is formal and clear.

questions.q: Which counts as experience on a CV?
questions.explain: Volunteering shows skills and reliability.

questions.q: Put the covering letter in order.
items: Which job you are applying for
questions.explain: Address and date, greeting, the job, why you suit it, closing.

reflect.q: What will you add to your CV?

units.parent: Your child learned to write a CV and a covering letter.
units.teacher: Shows knowledge of CV structure, covering letter format and formal register.
units.done: Keep your CV short and clear, and tailor each covering letter.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Critical language awareness
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 English Home Language: Language Structures and Conventions; Reading and Viewing (critical language awareness: denotation and connotation; emotive and manipulative language; bias)
units.intention: Today I am noticing how word choice shapes what we think.
units.prompt: Where have you seen loaded language in the news?

lesson.say: Denotation is a word's dictionary meaning. Connotation is the feeling it carries. Slim and skinny both mean thin, but slim sounds positive and skinny can sound negative.
lesson.html:
slim 👍→thin→skinny 👎

Same denotation, different connotation.

lesson.say: Writers choose words to influence us. Protesters or rioters? Freedom fighters or rebels? The choice shows a point of view.
lesson.html:
protesters ↔ rioters→debate ↔ row→claimed ↔ explained

Ask: what other word could have been used?

lesson.say: Watch for generalisations like everyone knows, false choices like you're either with us or against us, and euphemisms that soften bad news, like let go instead of fired.
lesson.html:
Generalisation→False choice→Euphemism

Critical readers question the language.

example.q: Headline A: Community members gather to demand water. Headline B: Mob blocks road in water chaos. How do they differ?
steps: A uses neutral words: members, gather, demand.
B uses negative words: mob, chaos. It frames people as dangerous.

questions.q: Which word has a positive connotation?
questions.explain: Determined sounds positive.

questions.q: Which is a euphemism?
hints: A softer way to say something.
questions.explain: Passed away softens died.

questions.q: Everyone knows this school is the best. What technique is this?
questions.explain: It is a sweeping generalisation.

questions.q: What is denotation?
questions.explain: Denotation is the literal meaning.

questions.q: You either support this plan or you don't care about children. What is the problem?
questions.explain: It falsely limits the options to two.

units.parent: Your child learned how word choice and techniques like euphemism can shape opinions.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing denotation and connotation, and identifying loaded language, generalisation, false dilemma and euphemism.
units.done: Notice the feelings behind words, and question language that tries to manipulate.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Human digestion
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Life Sciences, Term 2: Animal nutrition (human digestive system; mechanical and chemical digestion; enzymes; absorption; balanced diet)
units.intention: Today I am following food through the digestive system.
units.prompt: Why do we need enzymes?

lesson.say: Food travels from the mouth, down the oesophagus, to the stomach, the small intestine, the large intestine, and out through the anus. The liver and pancreas help digestion.
lesson.html: Mouth→Oesophagus→Stomach→Small intestine→Large intestine

lesson.say: Mechanical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces, like chewing. Chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones the body can absorb.
lesson.html:
Amylase: starch → sugar→Protease: protein → amino acids→Lipase: fat → fatty acids

Bile from the liver emulsifies fats.

lesson.say: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine through villi, tiny finger-like folds that give a huge surface area. The large intestine absorbs water.
lesson.html:
🫁

Villi increase surface area for absorption.

example.q: Why does bread start to taste slightly sweet if you chew it for a long time?
steps: The sugar makes it taste sweet.

questions.q: Where are most nutrients absorbed?
questions.explain: Most absorption happens in the small intestine.

questions.q: Which enzyme breaks down starch?
questions.explain: Amylase digests starch.

questions.q: What does bile do?
questions.explain: Bile emulsifies fats into small droplets.

questions.q: What is the main job of the large intestine?
questions.explain: The large intestine absorbs water.

questions.q: Put the parts in the order food passes through.
hints: The stomach comes before the intestines.
questions.explain: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine.

units.parent: Your child followed food through the digestive system and learned the role of enzymes.
units.teacher: Shows sequencing the alimentary canal, explaining mechanical and chemical digestion, enzymes and absorption.
units.done: Enzymes break food into small molecules that are absorbed in the small intestine.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Population ecology
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Life Sciences, Term 3: Population ecology (population size; mark-recapture; growth curves; predator-prey, competition, symbiosis)
units.intention: Today I am learning how populations grow and interact.
units.prompt: What limits the growth of a population?

lesson.say: Scientists cannot count every animal. With mark-recapture, they catch and mark some, release them, catch again, and use a formula to estimate the total.
lesson.html:
N = (M × C) ÷ R

M = marked first, C = caught second, R = recaptured marked.

lesson.say: A population often grows slowly, then quickly, then levels off at the carrying capacity: the most the environment can support.
lesson.html:
Lag→Exponential growth→Stationary phase

This S-shape is a logistic or sigmoid curve.

lesson.say: Predators and prey affect each other's numbers. Species compete for resources. Symbiosis includes mutualism, where both benefit, commensalism, where one benefits, and parasitism, where one is harmed.
lesson.html: Predation→Competition→Mutualism→Commensalism→Parasitism

example.q: Researchers mark 40 fish. Later they catch 50, and 10 are marked. Estimate the population.

questions.q: 30 animals are marked. Later 60 are caught and 15 are marked. Estimate the population.
What is carrying capacity?
options: The largest population the environment can support
questions.explain: Carrying capacity is the maximum sustainable population.

questions.q: Oxpeckers eat ticks off buffalo. Both benefit. What is this?
questions.explain: Both benefit, so it is mutualism.

questions.q: A tick feeds on a dog's blood. What is this?
questions.explain: The tick benefits and the dog is harmed.

questions.q: If prey numbers fall, what usually happens to predators?
options: Their numbers fall after a while
questions.explain: Predator numbers fall after prey numbers fall.

units.parent: Your child learned how scientists estimate populations and how species interact.
units.teacher: Shows applying mark-recapture, interpreting growth curves and classifying ecological interactions.
units.done: Populations grow to their carrying capacity and are shaped by how species interact.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Human impact on the environment
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Life Sciences, Term 4: Human impact on the environment (atmosphere and climate change; water availability and quality; food security; loss of biodiversity; solid waste)
units.intention: Today I am analysing how human activity affects the environment and what can be done.
units.prompt: Which environmental issue affects your community most?

lesson.say: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat in the atmosphere. This enhanced greenhouse effect is warming the Earth, causing more droughts, floods and heatwaves.
lesson.html:
Fossil fuels→CO₂→Trapped heat→Climate change

South Africa's electricity comes mostly from coal.

lesson.say: South Africa is a water-scarce country. Water is threatened by pollution, wasteful use, alien plants that use a lot of water, and acid mine drainage.
lesson.html:
Pollution→Wastage→Alien plants→Mine drainage

Cape Town's 2018 drought showed how real Day Zero can be.

lesson.say: Habitat loss, poaching and alien species threaten biodiversity. Solutions include renewable energy, saving water, protected areas, recycling and removing alien plants.
lesson.html: Renewables→Save water→Protect habitats→Recycle

example.q: How do alien plants like eucalyptus affect water supplies?
steps: They use more water than many indigenous plants.
They reduce the water reaching rivers and dams.
Clearing them, as Working for Water does, increases water supply.

questions.q: Which gas is mainly linked to the enhanced greenhouse effect?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide is the main greenhouse gas from human activity.

questions.q: What is acid mine drainage?
options: Acidic water flowing from mines and polluting water
questions.explain: It is acidic, metal-rich water that pollutes rivers.

questions.q: Which is a renewable energy source?
questions.explain: Solar power is renewable.

questions.q: What is the main threat to rhinos in South Africa?
questions.explain: Poaching is the main threat to rhinos.

questions.q: Helps or harms the environment?
questions.explain: Fixing leaks and planting indigenous trees help.

units.parent: Your child explored how human activity affects climate, water and biodiversity, and what can be done.
units.teacher: Shows explaining the enhanced greenhouse effect, threats to water and biodiversity, and evaluating solutions.
units.done: Human activity affects climate, water and biodiversity, and we can reduce the harm.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Media and democracy
units.topic: Democracy and human rights: the role of the media
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Life Orientation: Democracy and human rights (role of the media in a democratic society; freedom of expression and its limits; responsible use of social media)
units.intention: Today I am exploring the role of the media in a democracy and how to spot false information.
units.prompt: How do you check if something online is true?

lesson.say: In a democracy, a free media informs citizens, holds leaders accountable and gives people a voice. Freedom of the press is protected in Section 16 of the Constitution.
lesson.html:
Inform→Hold accountable→Give a voice

Investigative journalism has exposed corruption in South Africa.

lesson.say: Freedom of expression does not cover propaganda for war, incitement of violence, or hate speech based on race, ethnicity, gender or religion that incites harm.
lesson.html:
No incitement→No hate speech→No propaganda for war

Rights have limits that protect others.

lesson.say: Before you share, check the source, look for the date, see if trusted outlets report it, and be wary of headlines designed to make you angry.
lesson.html:
Source?→Date?→Other outlets?→Emotional bait?

Pause before you share.

example.q: A WhatsApp message says schools will close tomorrow, with no source. What should you do?
steps: Check: who sent it originally? Is there an official source?
Look on the Department of Education's official channels.
Do not forward it until it is confirmed.

questions.q: Which section of the Constitution protects freedom of expression?
questions.explain: Section 16 protects freedom of expression.

questions.q: Which is NOT protected by freedom of expression?
questions.explain: Incitement to violence is not protected.

questions.q: What is a sign of fake news?
options: No source and an emotional headline
It has a date and author
questions.explain: No source and emotional bait are warning signs.

questions.q: How does the media hold leaders accountable?
options: By investigating and reporting what they do
questions.explain: Investigative reporting holds leaders accountable.

questions.q: Put the steps before sharing in order.
questions.explain: Pause, check the source, compare outlets, then decide.

reflect.q: What will you do before sharing?

units.parent: Your child explored the media's role in democracy and how to spot false information.
units.teacher: Shows understanding of media freedom, its constitutional limits and strategies to identify misinformation.
units.done: A free media protects democracy, and responsible citizens check before they share.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Applying for study
units.topic: Careers and career choices: admission and applications
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Life Orientation: Careers and career choices (requirements for admission to higher education; Admission Point Score; application processes and deadlines)
units.intention: Today I am learning how admission works and how to plan applications.
units.prompt: Which course would you like to apply for?

lesson.say: The National Senior Certificate has different pass levels. A Bachelor's pass is needed for most degrees. A Diploma pass is needed for diplomas. A Higher Certificate pass is the entry level.
lesson.html:
Bachelor's→Diploma→Higher Certificate

Each course also has its own subject requirements.

lesson.say: Many universities use an Admission Point Score, or APS. Each subject percentage earns points, and the points are added up. Each university calculates it slightly differently.
lesson.html:
80–100% = 7→70–79% = 6→60–69% = 5→…

Your Grade 11 final results are often used for early offers.

lesson.say: Applications usually open in the year before you study, and many close by September or earlier. Some universities charge a fee. The Central Applications Office in KwaZulu-Natal handles several institutions at once.
lesson.html: Research→Check APS→Gather documents→Apply before deadline→Track your application

example.q: A course needs APS 30 and Mathematics at 60%. Sipho has APS 32 and Mathematics 55%. Should he apply?
steps: He should work to improve Maths, apply, and also apply to a second-choice course.

questions.q: Which NSC pass is needed for most degrees?
questions.explain: A Bachelor's pass is needed for most degrees.

questions.q: What is an APS?
options: A score based on your subject results
questions.explain: It totals points earned from subject results.

questions.q: Which results are often used for early offers?
questions.explain: Grade 11 results are often used for provisional offers.

questions.q: Why apply to more than one course?
options: To have a backup if the first is full
questions.explain: A second choice gives you a backup.

questions.q: When do many applications close?
options: In the year before study, often by September
In December of the study year
questions.explain: Many close by September of the year before.

units.parent: Your child learned about NSC pass types, APS scores and applying for study.
units.teacher: Shows understanding of NSC pass levels, APS calculation, subject requirements and application timelines.
units.done: Know your pass level and APS, check subject requirements, and apply early with a backup.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Healthy relationships
units.topic: Development of the self in society
units.caps: CAPS Grade 11 Life Orientation: Development of the self in society (relationships: signs of healthy and unhealthy relationships; respect and boundaries; where to get help)
units.intention: Today I am learning the signs of healthy and unhealthy relationships.
units.prompt: What does respect look like in a friendship or relationship?

lesson.say: Healthy relationships, whether friendships or dating, include respect, trust, honesty, good communication, and space to be yourself and see other people.
lesson.html: Respect→Trust→Honesty→Communication→Independence

lesson.say: Warning signs include jealousy and control, checking your phone, isolating you from friends, put-downs, pressure, threats, or any kind of violence.
lesson.html:
Control→Isolation→Put-downs→Pressure→Threats

Abuse can be physical, emotional, financial or digital.

lesson.say: You have the right to set boundaries and to say no. If a relationship feels unsafe, talk to a trusted adult. In South Africa, the GBV Command Centre is on 0800 428 428, and Childline is on 116.
lesson.html:
Trusted adult→Counsellor→GBV Command Centre 0800 428 428→Childline 116

It is never your fault if someone abuses you.

example.q: Leila's partner demands her phone password and gets angry when she sees friends. Is this healthy?
steps: Demanding passwords and anger about friends are controlling behaviours.
Leila deserves respect. She can talk to a trusted adult or counsellor for support.

questions.q: Which is a sign of a healthy relationship?
questions.explain: Respecting boundaries is healthy.

questions.q: Which is a warning sign?
questions.explain: Extreme jealousy and control are warning signs.

questions.q: What is digital abuse?
options: Using technology to control or harass someone
questions.explain: Digital abuse uses technology to control or harass.

questions.q: What is the GBV Command Centre number?
questions.explain: The GBV Command Centre is on 0800 428 428.

questions.q: If you feel unsafe in a relationship, what should you do?
options: Talk to a trusted adult or helpline
questions.explain: Reach out to a trusted adult or helpline.

reflect.q: What matters most to you in a relationship?

units.parent: Your child learned the signs of healthy and unhealthy relationships and where to get help.
units.teacher: Shows identifying healthy relationship qualities, warning signs of abuse, boundary-setting and support services.
units.done: Healthy relationships are built on respect. You can always ask for help.

units.subject: English
units.title: Comparing viewpoints
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500): Reading (comparing ideas, opinions and how writers present them across texts)
units.intention: Today I am comparing what two writers think and how they persuade.
units.prompt: Should phones be allowed at school? Why?
units.passage:
Text A (from a principal's newsletter)

Phones have no place in the classroom. Every buzz breaks concentration, and every screen is a doorway to distraction. Since we began collecting phones at the gate, teachers report calmer lessons, and learners talk to each other again at break.

Text B (from a learner's blog)

Banning phones treats us like children. My phone is my dictionary, my calculator and, when the taxi is late, the only way to tell my gran I'm safe. Teach us to use them well; don't pretend they don't exist.

lesson.say: Read the passage, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Text A (from a principal's newsletter)

Phones have no place in the classroom. Every buzz breaks concentration, and every screen is a doorway to distraction. Since we began collecting phones at the gate, teachers report calmer lessons, and learners talk to each other again at break.

Text B (from a learner's blog)

Banning phones treats us like children. My phone is my dictionary, my calculator and, when the taxi is late, the only way to tell my gran I'm safe. Teach us to use them well; don't pretend they don't exist.

lesson.say: A viewpoint is the writer's opinion. Text A argues phones harm learning. Text B argues phones are useful tools and learners should be trusted.
lesson.html: Text A: keep phones out→Text B: teach good use

lesson.say: Compare not only what they think, but how they persuade. Text A uses evidence from teachers. Text B uses personal examples and an emotional appeal about safety.
lesson.html: Link your points: whereas, similarly, in contrast.

example.q: Compare the evidence each writer uses.
steps: Text A uses reports from teachers about calmer lessons.
Text B uses personal experience: dictionary, calculator, contacting gran.
Whereas Text A relies on what staff have observed, Text B draws on one learner's everyday needs.

questions.q: What is Text A's viewpoint?
options: Phones should be kept out of the classroom
questions.explain: Text A says phones have no place in the classroom.

questions.q: Which phrase in Text B appeals most to emotion?
options: 'the only way to tell my gran I'm safe'
hints: Which one makes you feel something?
questions.explain: Safety and family make an emotional appeal.

questions.q: 'Every screen is a doorway to distraction' is an example of…
hints: A screen isn't literally a doorway.
questions.explain: It says a screen is a doorway, without 'like' or 'as'.

questions.q: Which linking word shows contrast?
hints: Three of these add or compare.
questions.explain: 'Whereas' introduces a difference.

questions.q: Which statement is a fair comparison?
options: Text A focuses on learning in class, while Text B focuses on phones' everyday uses
hints: Check each claim against the texts.
questions.explain: It accurately contrasts their focus.

units.parent: Your child compared two writers' opinions and how each one persuades.
units.teacher: Shows identifying viewpoints and comparing how writers use evidence and language to persuade, using comparative connectives.
units.done: Compare what each writer thinks and how they persuade, linked with comparison words.

units.subject: English
units.title: Connotation and tone
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500): Reading (how word choice, connotation and tone shape meaning)
units.intention: Today I am exploring how word choices create tone.
units.prompt: Have you ever been upset by how something was said, rather than what?

lesson.say: Words have a dictionary meaning, called denotation, and associations, called connotation. Slim and skinny both mean thin, but slim sounds positive, and skinny can sound negative.
lesson.html: slim: positive→skinny: negative

lesson.say: Tone is the writer's attitude, shown through word choice. It might be angry, admiring, sarcastic, nostalgic or hopeful.
lesson.html: Name the tone, then quote the words that create it.

lesson.say: Pick a word, give its connotations, link them to the tone, and say how the reader is meant to feel.
lesson.html: Word→Connotations→Tone→Reader's response

example.q: 'The developers bulldozed the old cinema.' What tone does 'bulldozed' create?
steps: Literally, a bulldozer knocks buildings down.
It suggests force, carelessness and destruction.
The tone is critical: the writer disapproves of the developers.

questions.q: Which word has the most positive connotation for someone careful with money?
hints: They all mean careful with money.
questions.explain: 'Thrifty' suggests sensible saving; the others sound critical.

questions.q: 'The so-called experts were wrong again.' What is the tone?
questions.explain: 'So-called' and 'again' mock the experts.

questions.q: 'We would sit on Gogo's stoep, the evening smelling of rain and woodsmoke.' What is the tone?
questions.explain: It looks back fondly on the past: nostalgic.

questions.q: What is connotation?
options: The associations and feelings a word carries
questions.explain: Connotation is what a word suggests beyond its dictionary meaning.

questions.q: Which word suggests a crowd is threatening?
questions.explain: 'Mob' suggests an angry, uncontrolled crowd.

options: Linking words to the reader's feelings

units.parent: Your child explored how word choice creates a writer's tone.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing denotation from connotation and analysing how lexical choices create tone.
units.done: Words carry feelings. Name the tone and quote the words that create it.

units.subject: English
units.title: Summary: concise and in your own words
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500): Reading and writing (summarising selected ideas concisely, fluently and in own words)
units.intention: Today I am writing a concise summary in my own words.
units.prompt: What time does your body want to sleep?
units.passage:
Why teenagers struggle to wake up (a 2to.iQ article)

Parents often blame late nights on laziness, but biology tells a different story. During adolescence, the body releases melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy, about two hours later than it does in childhood. A teenager who cannot fall asleep before eleven is not being stubborn; their body clock has genuinely shifted.

Screens make matters worse. The blue light from phones delays melatonin even further, and social media keeps the brain alert. Early school starts add to the problem, so many teenagers are always short of sleep.

Some schools that have moved their start time later report better attendance and fewer car accidents among teenage drivers. Simpler changes help too: switching off screens an hour before bed, and keeping wake-up times regular, even at weekends.

lesson.say: Read the passage, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Why teenagers struggle to wake up (a 2to.iQ article)

Parents often blame late nights on laziness, but biology tells a different story. During adolescence, the body releases melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy, about two hours later than it does in childhood. A teenager who cannot fall asleep before eleven is not being stubborn; their body clock has genuinely shifted.

Screens make matters worse. The blue light from phones delays melatonin even further, and social media keeps the brain alert. Early school starts add to the problem, so many teenagers are always short of sleep.

Some schools that have moved their start time later report better attendance and fewer car accidents among teenage drivers. Simpler changes help too: switching off screens an hour before bed, and keeping wake-up times regular, even at weekends.

lesson.say: First mark the points that answer the question. For why teenagers struggle to wake up, the reasons are a later body clock, blue light from screens, alert brains from social media, and early school starts.
lesson.html: Body clock shifts→Blue light→Social media→Early starts

lesson.say: Combine points into fluent sentences, use your own words where you can, and leave out examples, statistics and repetition.
lesson.html: Cut: 'A teenager who cannot fall asleep before eleven is not being stubborn.' That is an example.

example.q: Summarise the causes in one sentence.
steps: Point 1: the sleep hormone arrives later in adolescence.
Points 2 and 3: screens and social media keep them awake. Point 4: school starts early.
Teenagers' body clocks shift later, screens and social media delay sleep further, and early school starts leave them short of rest.

questions.q: Which is a reason teenagers struggle to wake up?
options: Melatonin is released later in adolescence
hints: The writer rejects one of these.
questions.explain: The later release of melatonin is a cause; the writer rejects laziness.

questions.q: For a summary of the CAUSES, which detail should be left out?
options: Fewer car accidents at schools that start later
hints: It is a result of a solution.
questions.explain: Fewer accidents is a result of later starts, not a cause.

questions.q: Which is the most concise own-words version of 'the body releases melatonin … about two hours later than it does in childhood'?
options: The body releases melatonin about two hours later than in childhood.
Melatonin, a hormone, which is the hormone that makes us sleepy, comes later.
questions.explain: It keeps the meaning in fewer, original words.

questions.q: What should you do with ideas that are repeated?
questions.explain: Combine repeated ideas to stay concise.

questions.q: Which is a suggested solution, not a cause?
options: Switching off screens an hour before bed
questions.explain: Switching off screens is a way to help, not a cause.

units.parent: Your child wrote a concise summary of an article in their own words.
units.teacher: Shows selecting points for a specific focus, excluding examples and repetition, and writing fluently in own words.
units.done: Keep only what the question asks for, cut examples, and combine ideas in your own words.

units.subject: English
units.title: Argumentative writing
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500): Composition (argumentative writing: structure, development of ideas and counter-argument)
units.intention: Today I am building a strong argument, including the other side.
units.prompt: What change at school would you argue for?

lesson.say: An argument takes a clear position and supports it with reasons. State your view in the introduction, so the reader knows where you stand.
lesson.html: Thesis: Schools should start at nine, not half past seven.

lesson.say: Each paragraph makes one point, supports it with evidence or an example, then explains why it matters.
lesson.html: Point→Evidence→Explain

lesson.say: Strong arguments deal with the other side. Present an objection fairly, then answer it with a reason.
lesson.html: Some argue later starts mean later finishes; however, rested learners learn faster.

example.q: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph supporting later school starts.
steps: Choose one reason: sleep and learning.
'Starting later would let teenagers' body clocks work with learning, not against it.'

questions.q: Which is a clear thesis statement?
options: School uniforms should be optional in Grades 10 to 12.
Some people like uniforms and some don't.
hints: Which one says what should happen?
questions.explain: It states a clear, arguable position.

questions.q: What is a counter-argument?
options: An opposing view you present and then answer
questions.explain: You present the other side fairly, then rebut it.

questions.q: Which phrase best introduces a rebuttal?
hints: A rebuttal turns against the objection.
questions.explain: 'However' signals you are answering the objection.

questions.q: What should follow evidence in a paragraph?
options: An explanation of why it supports your point
questions.explain: Explain how the evidence proves your point.

questions.q: Which conclusion is strongest?
options: 'A later start is a small change that would give us healthier, sharper learners: it is time to try it.'
'In conclusion, I have written an essay.'
questions.explain: It restates the argument and ends with a call to act.

units.parent: Your child practised building an argument, including answering the other side.
units.teacher: Shows formulating a thesis, structuring paragraphs with evidence and explanation, and handling counter-arguments.
units.done: Clear position, one point per paragraph, answer the other side, end strongly.

units.subject: English
units.title: Narrative writing: building tension
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500): Composition (narrative writing: structure, characterisation, tension and endings)
units.intention: Today I am shaping a story and building tension.
units.prompt: What makes you keep reading a story?

lesson.say: A short story needs a clear shape: an opening that hooks, rising tension, a climax and a resolution. In a short piece, keep to a few characters and one main event.
lesson.html: Hook→Rising tension→Climax→Resolution

lesson.say: Slow time down at key moments. Use short sentences, sensory detail and information you hold back, so the reader is anxious to know what happens.
lesson.html: The handle turned. Slowly. Then stopped.

lesson.say: A good ending feels earned. It can resolve the problem, surprise the reader, or leave a meaningful question, but it should never feel rushed.
lesson.html: Avoid: 'And then I woke up. It was all a dream.'

example.q: Rewrite to build tension: 'I heard a noise and went to see what it was.'
steps: Slow it down and add sensory detail.
'A scrape. Then silence. I put down my pen and listened, my heart loud in my ears.'

questions.q: Which opening hooks the reader best?
options: 'Nobody believed Thabo when he said the river was rising.'
'This is a story about a boy.'
'Once upon a time there was a day.'
'I will now tell you a story.'
hints: Which makes you want to know more?
questions.explain: It raises a question and hints at danger.

questions.q: Which technique builds tension?
options: Short sentences at a key moment
questions.explain: Short sentences slow the moment and raise suspense.

questions.q: What is the climax of a story?
options: The moment of greatest tension or the turning point
questions.explain: The climax is the peak of tension.

questions.q: Why should a short story have only a few characters?
options: So each can be developed in the space available
questions.explain: Fewer characters can be developed properly.

questions.q: Which ending is weakest?
options: 'Then I woke up and it was all a dream.'
An ending that resolves the main problem
An ending with a meaningful surprise
An ending that leaves a thoughtful question
hints: Which one cancels the whole story?
questions.explain: The dream ending cancels the story instead of resolving it.

units.parent: Your child practised shaping a story and building tension.
units.teacher: Shows structuring narrative, controlling pace to build tension, and crafting effective openings and endings.
units.done: Hook, build tension, reach a climax, and end in a way the story has earned.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Solving quadratic equations
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580): Algebra and graphs (solving quadratic equations by factorising and by the quadratic formula)
units.intention: Today I am solving quadratic equations.
units.prompt: Why might an equation have two answers?

lesson.say: A quadratic equation has an x squared term. Make one side zero, then factorise. If two brackets multiply to give zero, one of them must be zero.
When it won't factorise, use the formula: x equals minus b, plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4 a c, all over 2 a.
Most quadratic equations have two solutions. Check both by substituting them back into the equation.

example.q: Solve x² − x − 12 = 0.
steps: Find two numbers that multiply to −12 and add to −1: −4 and 3.

questions.q: Factorise x² + 7x + 10.
questions.explain: 5 and 2 multiply to 10 and add to 7.
x − 3 = 0 gives 3; x + 6 = 0 gives −6.

questions.q: Solve x² − 9 = 0.
In 2x² + 3x − 5 = 0, what is the value of b² − 4ac?
Using the formula, what are the solutions of 2x² + 3x − 5 = 0?

units.parent: Your child solved quadratic equations by factorising and with the formula.
units.teacher: Shows solving quadratic equations by factorisation and by the quadratic formula, and checking solutions.
units.done: Make one side zero, factorise or use the formula, and expect two answers.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Composite and inverse functions
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580), Extended: Functions (function notation; composite functions; inverse functions)
units.intention: Today I am combining and reversing functions.
units.prompt: What everyday actions can be undone, and which can't?

lesson.say: f of x means a rule applied to x. If f of x is 2x plus 3, then f of 4 is 2 times 4 plus 3, which is 11.
f g of x means do g first, then f. If g of x is x squared, then f g of 3 is f of 9, which is 21.
lesson.html: x = 3→g: 9→f: 21

lesson.say: The inverse function, f to the minus 1, undoes f. Write y equals f of x, swap x and y, then make y the subject.

example.q: f(x) = 3x − 1. Find f⁻¹(x).
steps: Write y = 3x − 1, then swap x and y: x = 3y − 1.

questions.q: f(x) = 5x − 2. Find f(3).
f(x) = x + 4 and g(x) = 2x. Find fg(3).
f(x) = x + 4 and g(x) = 2x. Find gf(3).
questions.explain: f(3) = 7, then g(7) = 14. The order matters.

questions.q: f(x) = 2x + 3. What is f⁻¹(x)?
hints: Undo the steps in reverse order.
questions.explain: Undo +3 first, then ×2: (x − 3) ÷ 2.

questions.q: If f(5) = 12, what is f⁻¹(12)?
questions.explain: f⁻¹ reverses f, so f⁻¹(12) = 5.

units.parent: Your child combined functions and found inverse functions.
units.teacher: Shows evaluating functions, forming composite functions in the correct order, and finding inverse functions.
units.done: fg(x): g first, then f. The inverse undoes the function.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Vectors
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580): Transformations and vectors (column vectors; adding, subtracting and multiplying vectors by a scalar; magnitude)
units.intention: Today I am adding vectors and finding their length.
units.prompt: How would you give directions using only across and up?

lesson.say: A vector has size and direction. A column vector shows how far to move across, then up. In these lessons we write it in a line: 3, minus 2 means 3 to the right and 2 down.
lesson.html:
(3, −2): 3 right, 2 down

In a column vector, the top number is across and the bottom number is up.

lesson.say: To add vectors, add the top numbers and add the bottom numbers. 3, minus 2 plus 1, 5 gives 4, 3. To multiply by a number, multiply both parts.
The magnitude is the length of the vector. Use Pythagoras: the square root of across squared plus up squared. The vector 3, 4 has magnitude 5.

questions.q: What does the vector (−4, 1) mean?
questions.explain: −4 across is 4 left; 1 is 1 up.

questions.q: Find the magnitude of the vector (6, 8).

units.parent: Your child added and scaled vectors and found their length.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting column vectors, performing vector addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, and calculating magnitude.
units.done: Work part by part, and use Pythagoras for the magnitude.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: The sine and cosine rules
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580), Extended: Trigonometry (sine rule and cosine rule in triangles that are not right-angled)
units.intention: Today I am solving triangles that are not right-angled.
units.prompt: How could a surveyor measure across a river without crossing it?

lesson.say: The sine and cosine rules work in any triangle, not only right-angled ones. Label the sides a, b and c, opposite the angles A, B and C.
lesson.html: Side a is opposite angle A.

lesson.say: Use the sine rule when you know a side and the angle opposite it. a over sin A equals b over sin B equals c over sin C.
lesson.html: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C

lesson.say: Use the cosine rule when you know two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides. a squared equals b squared plus c squared minus 2 b c cos A.
lesson.html: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A

example.q: b = 5 cm, c = 8 cm and A = 60°. Find a.

questions.q: You know two sides and the angle between them. Which rule finds the third side?
hints: The angle is between the two sides.
That matches a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.
questions.explain: Two sides and the included angle: use the cosine rule.

questions.q: You know angle A, angle B and side a. Which rule finds side b?
hints: You have a side and its opposite angle.
questions.explain: A side with its opposite angle: use the sine rule.

questions.q: b = 3, c = 4 and A = 90°. Use a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A to find a. (cos 90° = 0)
questions.explain: a² = 25, so a = 5. With a right angle, the cosine rule becomes Pythagoras.

questions.q: a ÷ sin 30° = 10. What is a? (sin 30° = 0.5)
In triangle ABC, which side is opposite angle C?
hints: Sides are named after the opposite angle.
questions.explain: Side c is opposite angle C.

units.parent: Your child used the sine and cosine rules to solve triangles.
units.teacher: Shows labelling triangles, selecting the sine or cosine rule appropriately, and substituting to find sides.
units.done: Matching side and angle: sine rule. Two sides and the angle between: cosine rule.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Probability with tree diagrams
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580): Probability (tree diagrams; combined events; probability with and without replacement)
units.intention: Today I am using tree diagrams for combined events.
units.prompt: Does taking a sweet out of a bag change the chances for the next person?

lesson.say: A tree diagram shows two or more events one after the other. Multiply along the branches to find the probability of a path.
lesson.html: P(A then B) = P(A) × P(B)

lesson.say: When more than one path gives the outcome you want, add the probabilities of those paths.
lesson.html: P(one red) = P(red, blue) + P(blue, red)

lesson.say: If you don't put the first item back, the probabilities on the second branches change, because there is one item fewer in the bag.

example.q: A bag has 4 green counters and 1 yellow counter. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(both green).
steps: Second green: 3/4, because one green counter is gone.

questions.q: P(rain) = 0.3 each day, independently. What is P(rain on both of two days)?
A coin is tossed twice. What is P(two tails)?
A bag has 2 red and 3 blue counters. One is taken and not replaced. If it was red, what is P(the second is red)?
questions.explain: 1 red out of 4 remaining = 1/4.

questions.q: A bag has 2 red and 3 blue counters. Two are taken without replacement. What is P(red, then red)?
On a tree diagram, when do you add probabilities?
options: When several paths give the outcome you want
questions.explain: Multiply along a path; add the paths that give the outcome.

units.parent: Your child used tree diagrams to find probabilities of combined events.
units.teacher: Shows constructing and using tree diagrams, including conditional probability without replacement.
units.done: Multiply along a path, add between paths, and adjust without replacement.

units.subject: Combined Science
units.title: Enzymes
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Combined Science (0653): Biology (enzymes as biological catalysts; effects of temperature and pH)
units.intention: Today I am finding out how enzymes work and what stops them.
units.prompt: Why does a high fever make people so ill?

lesson.say: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living things without being used up. Each enzyme fits a particular substrate, like a lock and key.
lesson.html: Substrate→Fits the active site→Products

lesson.say: Enzymes work best at an optimum temperature, about 37 degrees Celsius in humans. Above this, the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured.
lesson.html: Denatured: the shape is lost, and it can't work again.

lesson.say: Each enzyme also has an optimum pH. Pepsin in the stomach works best in acid, while enzymes in the small intestine work best in slightly alkaline conditions.
lesson.html: Pepsin: acidic→Intestine enzymes: alkaline

example.q: Explain why an enzyme stops working at 70 °C.
steps: High temperature changes the shape of the active site.
The enzyme is denatured, so the reaction stops.

questions.q: What are enzymes?
options: Proteins that act as biological catalysts
questions.explain: Enzymes are protein catalysts.

questions.q: What does denatured mean?
options: The active site has changed shape permanently
questions.explain: Denaturing permanently changes the active site's shape.

questions.q: What happens to enzyme activity at low temperatures?
options: It slows down, but the enzyme is not denatured
questions.explain: Cold slows enzymes, but they recover when warmed.

questions.q: Why does each enzyme work on only one substrate?
options: Only that substrate fits its active site
questions.explain: The active site's shape fits only its substrate.

questions.q: What is the optimum temperature of most human enzymes, in °C?
questions.explain: Human body temperature, about 37 °C.

units.parent: Your child learnt how enzymes speed up reactions and what stops them working.
units.teacher: Shows explaining enzyme specificity and the effects of temperature and pH, including denaturation.
units.done: Enzymes fit their substrate. Too hot or the wrong pH changes their shape.

units.subject: Combined Science
units.title: Photosynthesis and respiration
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Combined Science (0653): Biology (photosynthesis; limiting factors; aerobic respiration)
units.intention: Today I am comparing how plants make food and how all living things release energy.
units.prompt: Where does the mass of a tree come from?

lesson.say: Plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll. Oxygen is released.
lesson.html:
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

Needs light and chlorophyll.

lesson.say: The rate of photosynthesis can be limited by light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature. Increasing whichever is in shortest supply speeds it up.
lesson.html: Light→Carbon dioxide→Temperature

lesson.say: All living cells respire to release energy. Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water. It is not the same as breathing.
lesson.html:
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

Energy is released.

example.q: A greenhouse farmer adds carbon dioxide on bright days. Why?
steps: On bright days, light is not the limiting factor.
Carbon dioxide may then limit the rate.
Adding it increases photosynthesis, so the plants grow faster.

questions.q: Which gas do plants take in for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide is used to make glucose.

questions.q: What absorbs light energy in a leaf?
questions.explain: Chlorophyll absorbs light.

questions.q: What are the products of aerobic respiration?
hints: It is the reverse of photosynthesis.
Carbon dioxide and water come out.
questions.explain: Respiration produces carbon dioxide and water.

questions.q: A plant is in dim light with plenty of carbon dioxide. What is the limiting factor?
questions.explain: Dim light limits the rate.

questions.q: Which statement is true?
options: Plants respire all the time, day and night
Respiration is the same as breathing
questions.explain: All living cells respire all the time.

units.parent: Your child compared photosynthesis and respiration, and what limits plant growth.
units.teacher: Shows stating the word equations for photosynthesis and aerobic respiration, and applying limiting factors.
units.done: Plants make glucose with light; every living cell respires to release energy.

units.subject: Combined Science
units.title: Acids, bases and salts
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Combined Science (0653): Chemistry (the pH scale; neutralisation; preparing and naming salts)
units.intention: Today I am using the pH scale and naming salts.
units.prompt: Why do people take antacids for heartburn?

lesson.say: pH measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, and above 7 is alkaline. Universal indicator changes colour across the scale.
lesson.html: Below 7: acidic→7: neutral→Above 7: alkaline

lesson.say: An acid reacts with a base to make a salt and water. This is neutralisation. Farmers add lime to acidic soil for this reason.
lesson.html: acid + base → salt + water

lesson.say: A salt's name comes from the metal in the base and the acid used. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid makes sulfates, and nitric acid makes nitrates.
lesson.html: Hydrochloric: chloride→Sulfuric: sulfate→Nitric: nitrate

example.q: Name the salt made when sodium hydroxide reacts with hydrochloric acid.
steps: The metal comes from the base: sodium.
The salt is sodium chloride; water is also made.

questions.q: A solution has pH 3. What is it?
questions.explain: pH 3 is below 7, so acidic.

questions.q: What are the products of neutralisation?
questions.explain: Acid + base → salt + water.

questions.q: Which salt is made from copper oxide and sulfuric acid?
questions.explain: Copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water.

questions.q: What pH is a neutral solution?
questions.explain: Neutral is pH 7.

questions.q: Why might a farmer add lime to soil?
options: To make the soil more acidic
questions.explain: Lime neutralises acidic soil so crops grow better.

units.parent: Your child used the pH scale and named the salts made in neutralisation.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting pH, describing neutralisation and naming salts from given acids and bases.
units.done: Below 7 acid, above 7 alkali. Acid + base → salt + water.

units.subject: Combined Science
units.title: Electric circuits
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Combined Science (0653): Physics (current, potential difference and resistance; series and parallel circuits)
units.intention: Today I am working out current, voltage and resistance.
units.prompt: Why do the other lights stay on when one bulb in your house blows?

lesson.say: Current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes with an ammeter connected in series. Voltage, or potential difference, is measured in volts with a voltmeter connected in parallel.
lesson.html: Current: ammeter, in series→Voltage: voltmeter, in parallel

lesson.say: Resistance opposes the current. Voltage equals current times resistance, so resistance is voltage divided by current, measured in ohms.
lesson.html: V = I × R, so R = V ÷ I

lesson.say: In a series circuit, the current is the same everywhere and the voltages add up. In a parallel circuit, each branch gets the full voltage, and the currents in the branches add up.
lesson.html: Series: same current→Parallel: same voltage

example.q: A lamp has 6 V across it and 0.5 A through it. Find its resistance.

questions.q: A resistor has 12 V across it and 3 A through it. What is its resistance, in ohms?
A 10 Ω resistor carries 2 A. What is the voltage across it, in volts?
How is an ammeter connected?
hints: It measures the flow through the circuit.
The current must go through it.
questions.explain: An ammeter goes in series so the current passes through it.

questions.q: Two identical lamps are in parallel with a 6 V battery. What is the voltage across each?
questions.explain: Each parallel branch gets the full 6 V.

questions.q: In a series circuit, if one lamp breaks…
questions.explain: A break in the only path stops the current everywhere.

units.parent: Your child worked out current, voltage and resistance, and compared series and parallel circuits.
units.teacher: Shows applying V = IR, connecting meters correctly, and describing current and voltage in series and parallel circuits.
units.done: V = I × R. Series shares the voltage; parallel shares the current.

units.subject: Combined Science
units.title: Properties of waves
units.caps: Cambridge IGCSE Combined Science (0653): Physics (transverse and longitudinal waves; amplitude, wavelength and frequency; the wave equation)
units.intention: Today I am describing waves and using the wave equation.
units.prompt: How does sound reach your ears?

lesson.say: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. Amplitude is the height from the middle to a peak. Wavelength is the distance from one peak to the next. Frequency is the number of waves each second, in hertz.
lesson.html: Amplitude→Wavelength→Frequency (Hz)

lesson.say: In transverse waves, like light and water waves, the vibrations are at right angles to the direction the wave travels. In longitudinal waves, like sound, the vibrations are along the direction of travel.
lesson.html: Transverse: light, water→Longitudinal: sound

lesson.say: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength. A wave with frequency 5 hertz and wavelength 2 metres travels at 10 metres per second.
lesson.html: v = f × λ

example.q: A sound wave has frequency 170 Hz and wavelength 2 m. Find its speed.

questions.q: What do waves transfer?
hints: A cork on a ripple bobs up and down.
It doesn't travel with the wave.
questions.explain: Waves carry energy; the material just vibrates in place.

questions.q: Which is a longitudinal wave?
hints: Vibrations along the direction of travel.
questions.explain: Sound is longitudinal; the others are transverse.

questions.q: A wave has frequency 4 Hz and wavelength 3 m. What is its speed, in m/s?
What is the frequency of a wave?
options: The number of waves passing a point each second
questions.explain: Frequency is waves per second (Hz).

questions.q: A water wave travels at 6 m/s with wavelength 2 m. What is its frequency, in Hz?

units.parent: Your child described waves and used the wave equation.
units.teacher: Shows describing wave properties, distinguishing transverse and longitudinal waves, and applying v = fλ.
units.done: Waves carry energy. v = f × λ.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Functions in context
units.caps: IEB Mathematics (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 11 functions, with emphasis on interpreting graphs and parameters in real contexts
units.intention: Today I am interpreting a parabola in a real situation.
units.prompt: What shape does a ball make when you throw it?

lesson.say: The height of a ball is h equals minus 5 t squared plus 20 t, where t is time in seconds. The negative sign means the parabola opens downwards: the ball goes up, then comes down.
The turning point is the maximum height. The t-intercepts show when the ball is at ground level. Always say what each point means in the context.
lesson.html: Turning point: highest point→t-intercepts: on the ground

lesson.say: For a parabola a t squared plus b t, the turning point is at t equals minus b over 2a. Here that is minus 20 over minus 10, which is 2 seconds.

example.q: Find the maximum height of h = −5t² + 20t.
steps: The turning point is at t = 2 s.

questions.q: Why does h = −5t² + 20t open downwards?
options: The coefficient of t² is negative
questions.explain: A negative t² coefficient makes the parabola open downwards.

questions.q: At what time is the ball at its highest, in seconds?
When does the ball land? Solve −5t² + 20t = 0 for t > 0, in seconds.
questions.explain: −5t(t − 4) = 0 gives t = 4 s.

questions.q: What does the turning point represent here?
options: The ball's maximum height and when it happens
questions.explain: It gives the maximum height and its time.

questions.q: Why is only t > 0 sensible here?
options: Time after the throw can't be negative
It is a rule of algebra
questions.explain: In this context, time starts at 0.

units.parent: Your child used a parabola to work out the height and flight time of a ball.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting a quadratic model, finding and interpreting turning points and roots, and applying contextual restrictions.
units.done: Every key point on the graph means something in the real situation.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Probability: dependent or independent?
units.caps: IEB Mathematics (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 11 probability: Venn diagrams, independent and mutually exclusive events, with justification
units.intention: Today I am deciding whether events are independent, and proving it.
units.prompt: Does today's weather change the chance of tomorrow's?

lesson.say: Two events are mutually exclusive if they can't happen together. Then P of A or B equals P of A plus P of B.
lesson.html: Mutually exclusive: P(A and B) = 0

lesson.say: Two events are independent if one doesn't change the chance of the other. Then P of A and B equals P of A times P of B.
lesson.html: Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

lesson.say: IEB questions often ask you to prove independence. Calculate P of A times P of B, and compare it with P of A and B. If they are equal, the events are independent.
lesson.html: Compare P(A) × P(B) with P(A and B).

example.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent?
steps: They are equal, so A and B are independent.

questions.q: P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0.15. Are A and B independent?
options: Only if they are mutually exclusive
questions.explain: 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15 = P(A and B), so they are independent.

questions.q: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent?
questions.explain: 0.3 ≠ 0.2, so they are not independent.

questions.q: A and B are mutually exclusive. P(A) = 0.25 and P(B) = 0.4. Find P(A or B).
Can two events with non-zero probabilities be both independent and mutually exclusive?
hints: Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) > 0.
questions.explain: If both probabilities are above 0, the product can't be 0.

questions.q: Rolling a 6 on a dice, then tossing heads on a coin. These events are…
hints: Does the dice affect the coin?
questions.explain: One doesn't affect the other.

units.parent: Your child tested whether events are independent and proved it with calculations.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing independent and mutually exclusive events and justifying independence numerically.
units.done: Independent if P(A) × P(B) = P(A and B). Show the comparison.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Comparing a text and an image
units.caps: IEB English Home Language (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 11 comparative analysis of a written text and a visual source
units.intention: Today I am comparing how a poem and an image present the same idea.
units.prompt: Which tells a story better, a picture or words?
units.passage:
Inheritance (a 2to.iQ poem)

My grandmother's hands were maps:
rivers of blue under paper skin,
a scar where the paraffin stove
once argued with her.

She never wrote a letter in her life,
yet every recipe I know
is written in the margins of her palms,
and I am still learning to read them.

lesson.say: Read the source, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Inheritance (a 2to.iQ poem)

My grandmother's hands were maps:
rivers of blue under paper skin,
a scar where the paraffin stove
once argued with her.
