She never wrote a letter in her life,
yet every recipe I know
is written in the margins of her palms,
and I am still learning to read them.

lesson.say: Imagine a photograph: an old woman's hands, close up, holding a wooden spoon over a pot. The light falls on the lines and scars of her skin.
lesson.html: Image (described): close-up of an old woman's hands, holding a wooden spoon over a pot; light on the lines and scars.

lesson.say: Both present hands as carrying history. The poem uses metaphor, hands as maps and margins, while the photograph uses close-up framing and light. Compare the idea, then the methods.
lesson.html: Shared idea→Poem's methods→Image's methods

example.q: Compare how both texts present the grandmother's hands.
steps: Shared idea: her hands hold her life story and knowledge.
The poem uses the map and margin metaphors.
The image uses a close-up and light to draw attention to scars and lines.

questions.q: What does the metaphor 'my grandmother's hands were maps' suggest?
options: Her hands record her life journey
questions.explain: Her hands record where life has taken her.

questions.q: What does 'every recipe I know is written in the margins of her palms' suggest?
options: Her knowledge was passed on through doing, not writing
She wrote recipes on her hands
hints: Yet the speaker knows her recipes.
questions.explain: Her knowledge was passed down through cooking together.

questions.q: Which camera technique matches the poem's focus on detail?
questions.explain: A close-up mirrors the poem's attention to detail.

questions.q: Which sentence compares rather than just describes?
options: While the poem uses metaphor, the photograph uses light to reveal the same history.
questions.explain: It links the methods of both texts to one idea.

questions.q: What does 'I am still learning to read them' suggest?
options: The speaker is still discovering what the grandmother taught
The grandmother is still teaching reading
hints: Reading the palms is a metaphor.
questions.explain: The speaker is still understanding her grandmother's legacy.

units.parent: Your child compared how a poem and an image present the same idea.
units.teacher: Shows identifying shared themes across a written and a visual text and comparing literary and visual techniques.
units.done: Find the shared idea, then compare how each text presents it.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Evaluating an argument
units.caps: IEB English Home Language (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 11 critical reading: evaluating arguments and identifying fallacies
units.intention: Today I am testing whether an argument holds up.
units.prompt: Have you ever won an argument without really being right?

lesson.say: A sound argument makes a claim, gives reasons and supports them with evidence. Weak arguments skip the evidence or use tricks instead.
lesson.html: Claim→Reason→Evidence

lesson.say: A fallacy is a flaw in reasoning. An ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument. A false dilemma pretends there are only two options. A hasty generalisation draws a big conclusion from too few examples.
lesson.html: Ad hominem→False dilemma→Hasty generalisation

lesson.say: To evaluate, say whether the reasoning is sound, name any flaw, and explain how it weakens the argument.
lesson.html: Name the flaw, then explain why it weakens the argument.

example.q: 'You can't trust Thandi's idea about recycling; she drives a big car.' Evaluate.
steps: The claim attacks Thandi, not her idea.
This is an ad hominem fallacy.
Her car doesn't make her recycling argument wrong, so the reasoning is weak.

questions.q: 'Either we ban all phones, or learners will fail.' What fallacy is this?
questions.explain: It ignores other options, such as rules for phone use.

questions.q: 'My two cousins hated that school, so it's a terrible school.' What fallacy is this?
questions.explain: Two examples are too few for a big conclusion.

questions.q: 'He's only 16, so his views on climate change are worthless.' What fallacy is this?
questions.explain: It dismisses the person, not the argument.

questions.q: What makes an argument strong?
questions.explain: Strong arguments support reasons with reliable evidence.

questions.q: Which is the best evaluation?
options: The argument is weak because it attacks the speaker rather than answering her point.
questions.explain: It names the flaw and explains why it weakens the argument.

units.parent: Your child tested arguments for flaws in reasoning.
units.teacher: Shows analysing argument structure, identifying common fallacies and evaluating their effect on persuasiveness.
units.done: Check the claim, reasons and evidence, and name any flaw.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Data in tables
units.caps: IEB Life Sciences (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 11 scientific skills: interpreting tables, calculating percentages and drawing conclusions
units.intention: Today I am interpreting a data table and drawing a conclusion.
units.prompt: How would you show that a vaccine works?

lesson.say: A table shows data in rows and columns. Read the headings and units first. In this study, 1 000 people were vaccinated and 1 000 were not.
lesson.html:
Vaccinated: 1 000 people, 20 got sick.

Not vaccinated: 1 000 people, 150 got sick.

lesson.say: To compare groups, convert to percentages. 20 out of 1 000 is 2 percent. 150 out of 1 000 is 15 percent.
lesson.html: 20 ÷ 1 000 = 2%→150 ÷ 1 000 = 15%

lesson.say: A conclusion answers the aim using the data. The vaccinated group had a much lower rate of illness, so the vaccine reduced illness in this study.
lesson.html: Conclusion = answer to the aim + data.

example.q: By how many percentage points did vaccination reduce illness?

questions.q: 20 out of 1 000 vaccinated people got sick. What percentage is that? (Type the number only.)
150 out of 1 000 unvaccinated people got sick. What percentage is that? (Type the number only.)
Which conclusion is supported by the data?
options: In this study, vaccinated people were less likely to get sick.
questions.explain: It is supported and doesn't overstate the result.

questions.q: Why were the two groups the same size?
questions.explain: Equal group sizes make comparison fairer.

questions.q: Why is a large sample, like 1 000, useful?
options: It makes the results more reliable
It removes the need for a control
questions.explain: Large samples improve reliability.

options: Linking the conclusion to the aim

units.parent: Your child interpreted a data table and drew a careful conclusion.
units.teacher: Shows extracting data from tables, comparing groups using percentages and drawing evidence-based conclusions.
units.done: Read the headings, convert to percentages, and conclude with data.

units.subject: Life Sciences
units.title: Evaluating a health claim
units.caps: IEB Life Sciences (CAPS content, IEB assessment): Grade 11 nature of science: evaluating claims, sample size, controls and sources
units.intention: Today I am testing a health claim like a scientist.
units.prompt: Have you seen a health 'miracle' online?
units.passage:
Source: a social-media post (made up)

"Scientists PROVE that drinking 3 cups of rooibos tea a day stops heart disease! A study of 40 people found that tea drinkers had lower blood pressure after 2 weeks. Share before Big Pharma deletes this!"

lesson.say: Read the source, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Source: a social-media post (made up)

"Scientists PROVE that drinking 3 cups of rooibos tea a day stops heart disease! A study of 40 people found that tea drinkers had lower blood pressure after 2 weeks. Share before Big Pharma deletes this!"

lesson.say: How many people were studied? Was there a control group? How long did the study last? Who funded it? Was it published and checked by other scientists?
lesson.html: Sample size→Control→Duration→Source

lesson.h: What it does and doesn't show
lesson.say: Lower blood pressure after two weeks is not the same as preventing heart disease. A small, short study can suggest an idea, but it can't prove it.
lesson.html: Suggests ≠ proves.

example.q: Identify two weaknesses in the rooibos claim.
steps: The sample is small: only 40 people.
The study lasted only 2 weeks, but heart disease develops over years.
So it can't show that tea 'stops heart disease'.

questions.q: Why is a sample of 40 people a weakness?
options: It is too small to be reliable
questions.explain: Small samples are less reliable.

questions.q: Why is 2 weeks too short to support the claim?
options: Tea takes a month to brew
hints: The claim is about heart disease.
questions.explain: A 2-week study can't show long-term prevention.

questions.q: What is missing that would make the study more valid?
options: A control group that drank no tea
questions.explain: A control group lets you compare fairly.

questions.q: What is the problem with the word 'PROVE'?
options: One small study can't prove a claim
questions.explain: One small study can suggest, not prove.

questions.q: 'Share before Big Pharma deletes this!' is an example of…
options: an emotional appeal that avoids evidence
questions.explain: It uses fear and urgency instead of evidence.

units.parent: Your child evaluated a health claim like a scientist.
units.teacher: Shows evaluating scientific claims in terms of sample size, controls, duration and source reliability.
units.done: Ask: how many, compared with what, for how long, and who says so?

units.subject: Advanced Programme Mathematics
units.title: Proof by induction
units.caps: IEB Advanced Programme Mathematics: Module 1, Algebra (proof by mathematical induction)
units.intention: Today I am proving statements for every natural number using induction.
units.prompt: How do you know every domino in a row will fall?

lesson.say: Induction proves a statement for every natural number. Show the first case is true, then show that if any case is true, the next one is true too. Like dominoes, they all fall.
lesson.html: Base case→Assume true for k→Prove for k + 1→Conclude

lesson.say: Prove that 1 plus 2 plus up to n equals n times n plus 1 over 2. When n is 1, both sides are 1. Assume it is true for k.
Add k plus 1 to both sides. k times k plus 1 over 2, plus k plus 1, equals k plus 1 times k plus 2, over 2. That is the formula for k plus 1, so it is true for all n.

example.q: Check the base case of 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n².
steps: When n = 1, the left side is 1.
Both sides are equal, so the base case holds.

questions.q: What is the first step of proof by induction?
options: Show the base case is true
questions.explain: Start by proving the base case.

questions.q: In the inductive step, what do you assume?
options: The statement is true for n = k
It is true for all n
It is false for n = k
questions.explain: You assume it holds for n = k.

questions.q: What must you then prove?
options: That it is true for n = k + 1
That it is true for n = 1 again
questions.explain: Show that truth for k implies truth for k + 1.

questions.q: Why are both steps needed?
options: The base case starts the chain, and the step keeps it going
questions.explain: Without either step, the chain breaks.

units.parent: Your child learnt to prove statements for every number using mathematical induction.
units.teacher: Shows structuring a proof by induction: base case, inductive hypothesis, inductive step and conclusion.
units.done: Prove the first case, assume k, prove k + 1, then conclude.

units.subject: Advanced Programme Mathematics
units.title: Complex numbers
units.caps: IEB Advanced Programme Mathematics: Module 1, Algebra (complex numbers: arithmetic and solving quadratics)
units.intention: Today I am working with complex numbers.
units.prompt: What number squared gives −1?

lesson.say: There is no real number whose square is minus 1. We define i so that i squared equals minus 1. Numbers like 3 plus 2i are complex numbers.
lesson.html: i² = −1 · complex number: a + bi

units.intention: Today I am finding limits and testing whether a function is continuous.
units.prompt: Can you get closer and closer to something without reaching it?

lesson.say: The limit of f of x as x approaches a is the value f of x gets closer to as x gets closer to a. The function doesn't need to be defined at a itself.
lesson.html: lim (x → a) f(x)

lesson.say: Substituting x equals 2 into x squared minus 4 over x minus 2 gives 0 over 0. Factorise first: x minus 2 times x plus 2, over x minus 2, simplifies to x plus 2. The limit is 4.
lesson.html: (x² − 4) ÷ (x − 2) = x + 2 → limit as x → 2 is 4

lesson.say: A function is continuous at a if it is defined at a, the limit exists there, and they are equal. You could draw the graph there without lifting your pen.
lesson.html: f(a) defined→The limit exists→They are equal

example.q: Find the limit of (x² − 9) ÷ (x − 3) as x → 3.

questions.q: Find the limit of (2x + 1) as x → 3.
Find the limit of (x² − 4) ÷ (x − 2) as x → 2.
questions.explain: It simplifies to x + 2, so the limit is 4.

questions.q: Substituting gives 0 ÷ 0. What should you do?
questions.explain: 0 ÷ 0 means you should simplify first.

questions.q: Which is needed for f to be continuous at x = a?
options: f(a) is defined, the limit exists, and they are equal
That f is a straight line
questions.explain: All three conditions are needed.

questions.q: f(x) = 1 ÷ x. Is f continuous at x = 0?
questions.explain: f(0) is undefined, so f isn't continuous there.

units.parent: Your child found limits and tested whether functions are continuous.
units.teacher: Shows evaluating limits, resolving indeterminate forms algebraically and applying the definition of continuity.
units.done: Substitute; if you get 0 ÷ 0, simplify first. Continuous means defined, limit exists, and equal.
